full_text:
Hayden Large thought his football career might have ended in high school. Now he's bidding for a job with the Bears. Courtesy of the Chicago Bears
As Hayden Large and the rest of the Chicago Bears ran out of the tunnel Saturday for the preseason opener, his parents, Forrest and Jennifer, were in Section 132 in tears.
Forrest looked to his side and saw Large’s best friend and teammate at NAIA Dordt University, Brayton Van Kekerix, with his wife, Juliana. The former college linebacker was also in tears. Twenty-five of Large’s family and friends sat in Soldier Field — many in “88” Iowa jerseys. Not only did they watch Large play in an NFL preseason game, but he made the tackle on each of the team’s first two punts.
Seven years ago, no one would have thought this was possible.
“I don’t think he’d believe it,” Large said about his younger self a few days before his NFL debut.
It was the first time Large’s parents had attended a professional football game.
“To walk into a Bears game and have him out there was just, like I say, it was almost like time stopped,” Forrest said, “and it was just amazing.”
Large’s high school coach, Craig Tibbe, couldn’t make it. Unity Christian had its annual intrasquad scrimmage, the same one that in 2019 put Large’s athletic career in doubt.
Tibbe was frustrated at first. Here was his senior running back, who scored a 44-yard touchdown in their state championship win months earlier, fumbling on the very first play of the Blue-White scrimmage.
Forrest looked at Jennifer in the bleachers and said, “Oh s—.”
Large heard a pop. It’s a day he tries to “blank out,” but he remembers the sound. As he accelerated, he went down. Non-contact.
“I quickly went from being a little upset with him to, oh no, and feeling really bad for him,” Tibbe said. “And he was a guy who loved the team and loved the game.”
When Large asked the doctor if he could play again, the response was, “We’re gonna first focus on making sure you can walk without a limp naturally before we worry about ever playing football again.”
“That’s where we kind of realized that this injury was very uncommon and relatively severe for an athlete’s career,” Forrest said.
Large’s hamstring had torn a chunk of his pelvis off. The doctors had to create two braces for him — one that went around his waist because he couldn’t bend, and another on his leg to keep it bent, all done to keep pressure off the hamstring so it wouldn’t put pressure on the pelvic bone that was just reattached.
For five weeks, Large couldn’t sit or lie on his back. Standing required crutches. He couldn’t go to school. The Large family outfitted their living room to be his new bedroom because he couldn’t take the stairs. He was essentially bedridden for 35 days.
His high school football career was over. At that point, his goal was to make it back for basketball season. But he also wanted to support his teammates as they tried to defend their title.
The Large family put down the back seat in their Honda CR-V. He’d crawl in, and they would drive right up to the field, roll him out of the back and he would stand with crutches to watch high school football.
The first game came against Unity Christian’s rival. Large asked his dad, “Are you excited?”
Forrest’s response was tepid. “Yeah, kinda.”
“It’s just different when you’re not out there,” Forrest told him.
That’s when the competitor came out.
“What do you mean? This is still my team. This is our team,” Hayden said to his dad. “You better be just as excited as if I’m playing.”
“I’m like, dude,” Forrest recalled, “that’s pretty cool perspective.”
Hayden didn’t play a snap and still got a handful of votes for team MVP, a sign of what he meant to the program. But any college offers that came during his previous season were gone, except for one, at Dordt University in Iowa.
“He kind of has that air about him like, you want to pull for him, and you have confidence that he’s going to give you everything he has,” Tibbe said.
Forrest had two goals for Hayden’s high school career — score a touchdown on varsity and make a basket on varsity.
“Maybe my bar was set a little too low,” he said. “But I never wanted to put him beyond and I mean, he just took off his junior year and that’s when we decided he’s actually got some amazing talent.”
In the state title game, Large took a handoff from the throwback Wing-T offense for a touchdown.
“He was probably one of our best, what I call fakers,” Tibbe said. “He would hide the ball very well. He was a bigger-bodied fullback than we typically have, but he ran things so well; he was so smart, knew where blocks were coming from, would slide over, wait for that guy to slide in there and get the block and hid the ball well.
“He often would spring things when no one knew he had the ball. And he had a really weird ability of making people miss. It doesn’t look that agile, but man, he just … I don’t know, something about it in that game that was a big deal. Busting that thing and kind of set the tone for the rest of the night.”
What made the injury extra devastating was how hard Hayden had worked that summer to get ready for his senior season.
“It was gut-wrenching, to be honest,” Forrest said.
But then came basketball season, and Large received medical clearance. At first, he played with a bit of a limp, dragging the injured leg up and down the court, but eventually he felt like himself again — and decided to continue pursuing football.
“A s a parent, you never want to see … the injury was so traumatic,” Forrest said. “But I think he wanted to kind of prove to himself.”
Dordt provided the lifeline, and Large shockingly started his first game.
“My wife and I sat there and we just cried,” Forrest said.
Because Dordt was one of the few lower-level schools playing football in 2020, Large’s football career was back on track. Had he gone two full years without playing, that might have been it. He had 19 catches for 406 yards and five touchdowns in 2021. He had 316 yards on 19 catches the next season before landing an opportunity to be a preferred walk-on at Iowa.
With the Hawkeyes, Large had 14 career receptions and zero touchdowns, yet The Athletic ’s Dane Brugler wrote that Large was “described as the ‘heart and soul’ of that program.” Based on Brugler’s conversations with those around the program and in the NFL scouting community, he added, “His football character is off the charts — he will do whatever is needed, no questions asked.”
When Large hears that, he takes a second, letting the praise sit with him.
“It means a lot, those words,” he said. “That’s pretty cool to hear.”
Said Forrest, “I think there’s probably more pride in that statement than anything he’s done on the field.”
“Where does it come from? I don’t know,” Large said. “I’ve never been the most talented or most athletic guy, so I just wanted to always outwork people and just, the reason you play a game like this is for the people around you. It’s a selfless game that I fell in love with, and I’ll do what it takes for my teammates.”
That’s the intangible that Bears general manager Ryan Poles and coach Ben Johnson were trying to identify when building a rookie class. Johnson called Large before the draft to tell him they had a vision for him. The Bears took tight end Sam Roush in the third round but still wanted Large in the building.
“He didn’t bat an eye,” Johnson said in May. “This is where he wanted to be. To me, that speaks volumes about how he’s wired. That has something to do with how he came, walk on at Iowa, earning playing time and going through the long, hard road. I really appreciate that. I think we got a good one there.”
Center Logan Jones played with Large at Iowa and watched his journey from Dordt to Hawkeyes fullback to tight end and then to the Bears.
“His leadership, not only in the tight end room at Iowa, but on the team and the influence (he had); he wasn’t always the most vocal, but he did things the right way, and people rallied behind him and followed…

full_text:
Veteran Swayze Bozeman has helped bolster the Bengals' linebacker corps in training camp. Katie Stratman / Imagn Images
The Bengals’ three most notable positions of concern prior to the start of training camp were linebacker, cornerback and offensive tackle. Some might even throw running back into the mix on a slow news day.
Each of those positions experienced a boost of confidence or a seed of concern since players reported to camp three weeks ago . With less than four weeks to go before the Bengals’ season opener against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, let’s look at how each position has changed, potential options going forward and what matters over the next stage of camp.
In our annual fan survey , 74.8 percent of fans ranked this as the top positional concern heading into the season. The next closest position group was the offensive line, at 11 percent. No players with real experience were added to the linebackers room, and what the existing group’s film from last year would make the most optimistic fan hyperventilate.
Thus far, however, Cincinnati’s young linebackers have breathed new life into the position. The jury will remain out until Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight Jr. actually play a full game, but the initial results have been encouraging.
Carter and Knight look more confident so far this year. They’re commanding the defense pre-snap and they have made impressive plays in camp.
Defensive coordinator Al Golden heaped praise on many players, and he didn’t scale back his support for the two players he placed the biggest bets on during his tenure in Cincinnati.
“Command is night and day,” he said of Carter and Knight during the second week of practices.
Golden sees the two linebackers consistently making the correct adjustments and checks, and he has commended their use of the “empowerment” and “freedom” to align the defense the way they see it on the grass.
The confidence the organization hoped to see by betting on them has so far produced positive returns.
“I think they have something to prove,” Golden said. “I think they’ve got an edge.”
In addition to Carter and Knight, a new name has emerged beyond the starters: Swayze Bozeman.
Bozeman popped up on the second team after an extremely productive preseason debut for Cincinnati. The 27-year-old has logged nine tackles in nine NFL games over the last two seasons. The Bengals claimed him off waivers from the New York Giants in May, and he has made an impression in a room dominated by youngbloods.
If Swayze performs as well in the Bengals’ two remaining preseason games as he did Thursday against the Detroit Lions, he could earn a spot on the 53-man roster and provide some much-needed depth as the season begins.
The Lions game raised a crucial question about Cincinnati’s hopes this season. When undrafted free-agent rookie Eric O’Neill beat Orlando Brown Jr. around the edge for a hit on Joe Burrow, the Bengals were reminded of the tough spot they could be in if Brown regresses.
The team didn’t address the position in the draft or free agency, but the organization held on to tackle Cody Ford — who has lost 40 pounds — as a backup while giving him a pay cut.
Brown has had occasional rough moments during camp, but coach Zac Taylor wasn’t hitting the panic button after a dozen practices and two live series.
“I think he is motivated to give us the best version of himself,” Taylor said. “He’s been a strong leader on this team. Anytime something doesn’t go perfectly, he wears it and takes ownership for it. I think anytime Joe gets hit, all those guys are trying to figure out what they can do better. We all are. None of us want to be in that position. There are things we can always do to help those guys as well.”
What are those things? Well, if you are thinking one of them is adding an accomplished tackle in free agency, that’s unlikely to be the answer. Players at the same level or better than Brown aren’t sitting at home on Aug. 18.
Yes, the Bengals landed right guard Dalton Risner near the end of last August, but finding a similar player this year would be unlikely, and Risner’s path to becoming a starter in 2025 came at the expense of early-season issues.
Sure, you can point to names like Taylor Decker, Cam Robinson and Jonah Williams still being available, but the Bengals are not about to give up on Brown or Ford. Would any of those names willingly jump into a crowded situation? Are they healthy enough to do so even if they wanted to? Would either be an upgrade?
It’s more likely that a player like Javon Foster, who started taking second-team reps this week, will claim the fourth spot, or the Bengals could land a young player they like on the waiver wire or via a cutdown weekend trade.
All of these questions point back toward Brown and Ford being the answers at tackle. It would be nice to see Brown bounce back in the team’s joint practice with the Chicago Bears on Thursday, if only to reassure observers that the early poor reps won’t become a trend.
The depth chart feels much better at corner than it did before camp started. The Bengals can thank DJ Ivey for that. The 2023 seventh-round pick put together an impressive camp to solidify the third corner job.
With Dax Hill out with a soft-tissue injury, Ivey has seen his fair share of matchups against Tee Higgins and Ja’Marr Chase. The 26-year-old has also seen his fair share of wins.
There will be moments when Higgins high-points a Burrow pass in the corner of the end zone or pulls off one of those unguardable moves that made him one of the best in the game. The fact that Ivey has more than held his own against the best receiving combo in football goes a long way to allowing every other corner on the roster to fill a more appropriate role.
Tacario Davis has been solid, but landing as CB4 would be an appropriate starting spot for a third-round rookie. The same for Ja’Sir Taylor, competing at nickel corner but focusing on special teams, and Brayln Lux, attempting to land a roster spot by making a positive impression behind Jalen Davis in the nickel competition.
There’s still a projection involved with much of the depth here, but what we’ve seen suggests there are answers the coaches can trust. Those were built over the last three weeks.

full_text:
Jordyn Brooks led the NFL with 183 tackles last season with the Dolphins. Could he be a Cowboys target? Jeff Romance / Imagn Images
OXNARD, Calif. — Adding Von Miller is probably not the final notable move the Dallas Cowboys will make before the start of the regular season.
Miller and the Cowboys agreed on Sunday to a one-year, $5.5 million deal that’s worth up to $7.5 million. The 37-year-old gives Dallas a veteran pass rusher who believes he’s still capable of 8-10 sacks.
“Obviously you get someone that’s been there and done that,” Cowboys owner Jerry Jones said after Monday’s practice. “He trains with our consulting trainer. And boy, he had been telling us for this past year if we could get him, he knew he could help us. … We feel real good. He’s a veteran that can really bring a great aspect to the team concept. He really wants to be here. We want him here and we believe he can come in here and really give us some additional pressure on the other quarterback.”
While that likely closes the door on any more discussions of trading for Maxx Crosby, it doesn’t mean the Cowboys believe their defense is set. The offense has all the pieces to be one of the league’s best. The defense probably still needs another upgrade.
Jones said at the start of training camp that the Cowboys were open to making a “substantive” move. He said after Monday’s practice that those thoughts haven’t changed.
“Yes, if we had an opportunity, I would be (interested),” Jones said. “It’s as much about what I think of where we are, which I’m more positive than when we started camp, seriously, about what our chances are. And so I think if we saw an opportunity to take a little of the future and put it on this team, I’d do it if it would help us.”
As there was with Miller, there has been speculation regarding other free agents and the Cowboys. There has been outside chatter about linebackers Bobby Wagner and Bobby Okereke and a recent ESPN report about cornerback Adoree’ Jackson . Those names make sense because those are Dallas’ biggest positions of need at the moment.
But none sound like a “substantive” move.
Outside linebacker seems set now that the group includes Miller, Rashan Gary, Donovan Ezeiruaku, Malachi Lawrence and James Houston. Defensive tackle is probably in a similar spot with Quinnen Williams, Kenny Clark and Otito Ogbonnia. Safety is as secure as it has been in over a decade with Jalen Thompson, Caleb Downs, Malik Hooker and P.J. Locke.
Inside linebacker and cornerback still have questions.
If they were guaranteed full health, DeMarvion Overshown, Dee Winters, Jaishawn Barham, Shemar James and Justin Barron could be a solid group. But Overshown has only played in 19 games over the last three seasons. Barham is currently working his way back from a groin injury.
Cornerback also has its share of injury concerns with DaRon Bland and Shavon Revel coming back from notable injuries in recent years. Bland, Revel and Cobie Durant could be a good starting trio, but can they all stay healthy? Saturday’s preseason opener showed that the depth isn’t great at the position.
“I love our roster,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said Monday. “I really do. I think we’re a talented roster. We’re way different on paper this year than we were last year. But we’re not done. We’re not done developing our players. We’re not done getting the young guys ready to go. We’re not done potentially adding pieces.”
If a notable move is to be made, it’s likely at inside linebacker or cornerback.
• It’s difficult to project who could become available when teams start trimming their rosters to a final 53. A popular name in Dallas over the last few months has been Miami Dolphins linebacker Jordyn Brooks. Miami isn’t expected to be very good this season. Most sportsbooks have them at the bottom of the NFL 2026 win projections at 3-4 wins. Brooks is fresh off being named first-team All-Pro last season. Miami’s other starting linebacker, Tyrel Dodson, is another possibility if the Dolphins are looking to add draft picks.
• Cornerback could come down to a young player on another team stepping up in the preseason, making a veteran player a little more expendable. Starting corners who have been speculated as potential trade candidates this summer around the NFL include Kansas City’s Kristian Fulton and Denver’s Riley Moss.
The Cowboys might not do anything else, but they have done a good job of expressing how open they are to making a significant move if another team is looking for a partner.

ALLEN PARK, Mich. — Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said the preseason is where the roster will begin to separate. It’s when you find out how guys perform under the lights, and if what they’re being taught in camp can translate to games.
Where do things stand now that the preseason opener is in the books?
Time for a fresh 53-man roster projection.
The question here is whether or not the Lions carry two or three quarterbacks. Goff is the starter, and Dobbs feels as close to a lock as possible given the circumstances. Dobbs has been here for about a week, but he’s previously been with the organization, has known Goff for 15 years and has played for Drew Petzing. He’s perfect for what the Lions are looking for in a backup. To make carrying three QBs worth their while, though, Altmyer has to make the most of his opportunities. He was solid in his preseason debut, and he’s the most mobile quarterback of the three in camp, but the Lions could opt to stash him on the practice squad instead and continue developing him.
Reserves: Isiah Pacheco, Sione Vaki, Jacob Saylors
Cut: Jabari Small, Trayveon Williams, Raheem Blackshear
This room is far from healthy. Pacheco is dealing with an MCL sprain and will need more time before he’s ready to go. Vaki broke his nose and was poked in the eye (which was red for a week) in a practice, and just returned. Saylors hurt his ankle in the preseason opener. Also, Small missed the preseason opener.
When healthy, the room feels somewhat set. If the Lions go with four, it’ll likely be Gibbs, Pacheco, Vaki and Saylors. If it’s three, Gibbs, Pacheco and Vaki feel like locks.
Starters: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa
Reserves: Greg Dortch, Dominic Lovett
Cut: Tay Martin, Tarik Black, Cedrick Wilson Jr., Malik Cunningham, Tom Kennedy, Lucky Jackson
Campbell loves the depth in this room, but does it love it enough to roster six receivers? St. Brown, Williams, TeSlaa and Dortch are locks. Lovett can serve a purpose as an upside receiver with return ability behind Dortch, and rookie Kendrick Law’s injury makes it easier to justify. There’s an ongoing competition for the No. 6 spot, should the Lions choose to roster six. In the end, I think there could be room for one more, but there hasn’t been enough separation as of yet. My money would be on Martin. Campbell raved about him Saturday morning — particularly what he can add on special teams. But he has to keep stacking days.
Reserves: Brock Wright, Tyler Conklin
Cut: Jackson Meeks, Thomas Gordon, Zach Horton, Miles Kitselman
The Lions could go light at tight end again. LaPorta and Wright are locks, and you have to think Conklin is too after the team signed him this offseason. If there’s a case for a fourth, it could be Meeks. A 2025 UDFA wide receiver, the Lions moved Meeks to tight end late last year and liked what they saw. He returned for training camp this year as a full-time tight end and has looked explosive. He might need more time on task, which makes him a practice-squad candidate, but there’s upside here.
Starters (right to left): Blake Miller, Tate Ratledge, Juice Scruggs, Christian Mahogany, Penei Sewell
Reserves: Ben Bartch, Larry Borom, Miles Frazier, Seth McLaughlin
Cut: Mason Miller, Melvin Priestly, Michael Niese, Devin Cochran, Colby Sorsdal
The injury to Mays is a big one , as the Lions will be without their starting center and big free-agent addition until mid-to-late October. Have to think Scruggs is the favorite to start. He spent most of Saturday’s practice as Goff’s primary center. However, Mays’ injury opens the door for McLaughlin to make the roster as a reserve center.
Ratledge, Sewell and Miller are locks to start, and Mahogany and Bartch will battle it out for left guard.
Starters: Aidan Hutchinson, Tyleik Williams, Alim McNeill, Tyler Lacy
Reserves: D.J. Wonnum, Derrick Moore, Ahmed Hassanein, Levi Onwuzurike, Skyler Gill-Howard, Chris Smith
Cut: Payton Turner, Mekhi Wingo, Anthony Lucas, Tyre West, Eric O’Neill, Myles Adams, Ben Stille, Aidan Keanaaina
The surprise here is that Lacy is a projected starter, but he’s earned the majority of first-team reps dating back to OTAs and minicamp. The Lions love him in the big end role, and he can also kick inside and play some defensive tackle. Wonnum, Moore and Hassanein round out a solid edge room. Onwuzurike, Gill-Howard and Smith represent the DT depth behind Williams and McNeill. Smith was a toss-up, but the Lions could use some size after losing DJ Reader and Roy Lopez.
Starters: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Devin White or Malcolm Rodriguez
Reserves: Trevor Nowaske, Damone Clark
IR to return: Jimmy Rolder
Cut: Erick Hunter, Joe Bachie, Troy Reeder, Amen Ogbongbemiga
A deep room, especially when Rolder returns. The Lions know what they’re getting in Campbell, Barnes and Rodriguez. The organization kept six linebackers last year, so it makes sense for them to carry six again. Rolder appeared at practice Saturday afternoon but was mostly getting work in off to the side. Campbell said he’d need a minute. Clark has also missed time of late, but I’m keeping him here for now because of his special teams ability.
Starters: D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Christian Izien (nickel)
Reserves: Nick Whiteside, Ennis Rakestraw Jr., Keith Abney II (nickel), Khalil Dorsey, Roger McCreary
Cut: Aamaris Brown, Ryan Cooper Jr., Ekow Boye-Doe
Cornerback has to be one of the — if not, the — most concerning positions. Reed is coming off an injury-plagued season and is already dealing with a groin injury. Ya-Sin is entering his age-30 season. Rakestraw is trying to live up to his second-round draft status, and hasn’t been able to stay healthy. McCreary is an experienced veteran, but he’s had more downs than ups this training camp. And while Whiteside’s been one of the better players in camp, he doesn’t have much of a track record and is now dealing with a hamstring injury. There are a lot of unknowns here. The Lions are hoping it materializes.
Starters: Chuck Clark, Avonte Maddox
PUP: Kerby Joseph, Brian Branch
Clark and Maddox have been mainstays at safety since camp began. It doesn’t feel like they’re going to lose grip on their roles. Harper is in the mix as well as a reserve safety with starting experience. Izien has nickel/safety versatility, so you could include him here as well. Those four should be enough as the Lions slowly bring back Branch and Joseph — who could return in late August/early September.
Starters: Jack Fox (punter), Jake Bates (place kicker), Hogan Hatten (long snapper)
No surprises here. These three are locked in for the third consecutive year. One of the best specialist trios in the NFL.

full_text:
DJ Giddens entered camp with a chance to be Jonathan Taylor's top backup. Now he might not make the team. Michael Hickey / Getty Images
The end of an era is near. The Indianapolis Colts will host the Atlanta Falcons for a pair of joint training practices Wednesday and Thursday, marking their final two days of camp at Grand Park in Westfield, not just for this year but for the foreseeable future. The Colts, like the majority of other teams, will host training camp from their team facility starting next year.
As the Colts prepare for their last week of training camp, I took my first crack at projecting the team’s 53-man roster. NFL squads have until Aug. 30 to make their final roster decisions. Here’s who I think is making the cut:
In: Daniel Jones, Riley Leonard and Anthony Richardson Sr. Out: Easton Stick
Richardson’s trade request hasn’t been rescinded, but at this point, I’m leaning toward the 2023 No. 4 pick remaining with the Colts for the 2026 season. Yes, Jones is the team’s unquestioned starter, and while he’s recovered from his Achilles injury remarkably well, he still has a long injury history, so it doesn’t feel wise to simply trade Richardson away for, presumably, a Day 3 draft pick. He could still be useful in Indy, even if he loses the backup job to Leonard, especially when considering that the Colts, due to injury, started four QBs last year.
In: Jonathan Taylor, Seth McGowan (R), Ulysses Bentley IV Out: DJ Giddens, Anderson Castle (R), Roydell Williams (R)
Giddens, a 2025 fifth-round pick, is the odd man out at this position. He entered camp with a chance to be the backup behind Taylor, a three-time Pro Bowler, but a hamstring injury has sidelined Giddens for the majority of camp. In his absence, McGowan has flashed his physicality, and Bentley’s impressive hands out of the backfield have helped him build a strong case to win the job as Indy’s third-stringer.
In: Alec Pierce, Josh Downs, Ashton Dulin, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, Laquon Treadwell, Coleman Owen Out: Deion Burks (R), Anthony Gould, Sahmir Hagans (R), E.J. Horton (R), Eli Pancol, Raylen Sharpe (R), Ben Nikkel
Colts coach Shane Steichen said he doesn’t expect Pierce to practice against the Falcons this week, meaning he will miss all of training camp as he continues rehabbing from left ankle surgery. His absence has really exposed how thin the receiver room is behind him and Downs. That said, Dulin and Westbrook-Ikhine have flashed enough to be virtual locks to make the team. Treadwell and Owen seem riskier, but they offer more special teams experience than Burks, a rookie seventh-round pick. Gould does have some special teams prowess, though he’s currently sidelined due to a groin injury and hasn’t stood out much in camp.
In: Tyler Warren, Mo Alie-Cox, Drew Ogletree, Will Mallory Out: Pharaoh Brown, Carson Towt (R)
Mallory only appeared in two games last season, which was a career low for the 2023 fifth-round pick. But considering the Colts’ lack of receiver depth, it may behoove them to keep him around as a glorified wideout. Even though he’s received limited reps behind Warren, Alie-Cox and Ogletree in camp, he’s routinely made downfield catches that — with the help of some Steichen ingenuity — could translate to game days.
In: LT Bernhard Raimann, LG Quenton Nelson, C Tanor Bortolini, RG Matt Goncalves, RT Jalen Travis, G Jalen Farmer (R), C Dalton Tucker, T Luke Tenuta, T Blake Freeland Out: C Josh Kreutz (R), C Jimmy Morrissey, C Geno VanDeMark (R), G Josh Sills, T Bayron Matos, T Nolan Rucci (R)
Indy’s offensive line is one of the strongest units on the team, with its only new full-time starter being Travis. The 2025 fourth-round pick will take over for longtime stalwart Braden Smith, who is now with the Houston Texans. One could argue that I was a little greedy in keeping four more linemen once I moved past the starters of Raimann, Nelson, Bortolini, Goncalves and Travis. However, Colts GM Chris Ballard has always emphasized the importance of having depth in the trenches, which is why Freeland, the player I debated the most, made the cut. Tenuta appears to be the team’s third tackle, but since he left the preseason opener with a knee injury, it can’t hurt to have Freeland around as insurance. Farmer and Tucker also have clearly defined roles as second-stringers.
In: DE Laiatu Latu, DT DeForest Buckner, DT Grover Stewart, DE Arden Key, DE Micheal Clemons, DE Jaylahn Tuimoloau, DE George Gumbs Jr. (R), DE Caden Curry (R), DT Adetomiwa Adebawore, DT Colby Wooden Out: DE Mitchell Melton (R), DE Durell Nchami, DT Cameron Ball (R), DT Tim Smith, DT Jerry Tillery
Tillery was the hardest cut at this position because, again, Ballard values depth in the trenches. It’s also no secret that Buckner, who is returning from neck surgery, has been banged up in recent years. But with Wooden offering some positional versatility as a 3-tech and nose guard, I thought a spot for Tillery could be better used elsewhere. Gumbs and Curry make the cut as rotational pass rushers since the Colts don’t really have a full-time pass rusher opposite Latu.
In: CJ Allen (R), Bryce Boettcher (R), Akeem Davis-Gaither, Jaylon Carlies, Austin Ajiake Out: Tahj Chambers (R), Devin Veresuk, West Weeks (R)
The Colts have started several linebackers throughout training camp. Part of that constant rotation has been influenced by rookie second-round pick Allen, who has missed time due to calf and hamstring injuries. He’s back in the fold, but Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo recently indicated that the team could still utilize different linebacker tandems in different game-day situations.
In: Sauce Gardner, Charvarius Ward Sr., Justin Walley, Cam Taylor-Britt, Mekhi Blackmon, Johnathan Edwards Out: Jaylon Jones, Rob Carter Jr., Jai’Onte’ McMillan (R), Mekhi Rodgers (R)
Ward is sidelined indefinitely due to a back injury, which is very concerning since he was limited to just seven games last year after suffering three concussions. But assuming he’ll return for the start of the season, Indy’s cornerback room should be all but solidified. Walley is poised to start in the slot after missing his entire rookie season due to a torn ACL, and Taylor-Britt offers experienced depth behind him. Blackmon and Edwards started 11 and five games, respectively, last year and offer experience, too. Plus, Anarumo likes to deploy nickel and dime packages, which opens the door for more defensive backs to see the field.
In: Cam Bynum, A.J. Haulcy (R), Hunter Wohler, Jonathan Owens Out: Trey Washington, Juanyeh Thomas, Daniel Scott, Austin Brown (R)
Free safety Bynum headlines this position, and throughout camp he’s either been flanked by Haulcy or Wohler at strong safety. Haulcy appears to be on track to start, which shouldn’t be a surprise for the rookie third-round pick. Owens makes the cut thanks to his experience, positional versatility and special teams duties.
In: K Blake Grupe, P Rigoberto Sanchez, LS Luke Rhodes Out: K Spencer Shrader
Yes, Shrader drilled a 61-yard field goal in the Colts’ preseason opener, while Grupe missed his attempt from the same distance. Grupe, however, has still been much more accurate than Shrader in camp, and it doesn’t seem like Shrader has done enough overall to leapfrog his challenger.

title: Patrick Mahomes and Zach Ertz had same surgery — then became each other's motivator Here's how the Chiefs' QB and the NFL tight end linked up after knee injuries this offseason — and what they learned about each other. Jesse Newell
summary:

Less than 24 hours before his own knee surgery, tight end Zach Ertz picked up his phone to text Patrick Mahomes.

full_text:
Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes admitted his rehab from a serious knee injury could be "lonely." A connection with similarly injured tight end Zach Ertz helped. Jamie Squire / Getty Images
Less than 24 hours before his own knee surgery, tight end Zach Ertz picked up his phone to text Patrick Mahomes.
While watching football on television, Ertz had just seen the Kansas City Chiefs quarterback suffer a non-contact injury — and as someone who had gone through ACL recovery before, he knew what was coming next.
“It’s a lonely road ahead,” Ertz wrote to Mahomes, “but I’m here for you.”
Little did Ertz know at the time: Mahomes was about to be there for him as well.
Ertz and Mahomes — who previously knew each other from NFL offseason events — turned into critical support systems for each other this offseason, as both worked to push the limits of rehab after they went through ACL and LCL repair surgery on Dec. 15.
“It was good to have someone to just be like, ‘OK, where I’m at is right where I need to be.’ And we’re being aggressive, but we’re being smart,” Ertz told The Athletic last week. “So it was good to have someone that was constantly going through the same struggles that I was.”
Ertz, 35, injured himself a week before Mahomes last season while playing for the Washington Commanders. He immediately became emotional on the field, wondering whether that would mark the end of his playing career.
After he decided on surgery — and to pursue a comeback this year — Ertz said Mahomes helped him through the darkest days.
The two trained in different locations but motivated each other through text messages. It started with one of the most trying parts of rehab: the first month, which Ertz describes as “literally laying on a table and just cranking at your knee, trying to get the range of motion back.”
Back-and-forth texts with Mahomes kept his spirits up. How is your rehab going? How are you grinding through it? What did you work on today?
“It’s really just supporting one another,” Ertz said. “Truly happy for the other person’s progress because when you’re rehabbing, no one’s really there.”
Mahomes shared a similar sentiment at the start of this year’s training camp, saying his contact with Ertz was especially helpful through a “long process.”
“You feel like sometimes you’re lonely, because you’re doing stuff by yourself and you’re just competing against yourself,” Mahomes said. “So it gave me someone else I can compete with to push my competitive drive.”
Ertz says knee recovery is especially trying because progress can be non-linear — and improvement isn’t always instantaneous.
Football players are used to immediate feedback loops. Bench press one amount today and you can expect to do a little more tomorrow, then even more next week.
The knee rehab Ertz and Mahomes went through was completely different. You could be stuck at one weight on a leg exercise for a week because of a limited range of motion. And literally nothing you do — at least for a while — can even get you to a place where you can lift one pound more than you did previously.
“It’s tough not seeing those immediate results,” Ertz said. “And I think that is probably the toughest part, mentally just grinding through those difficult days where it’s not getting tangibly better objectively.”
Gains come over time, though, and Ertz said Mahomes was particularly helpful as the two were trending back in a similar way.
Ertz, for example, said he was hesitant at one point to attempt crossover steps as part of his rehab. Shortly after, though, he saw a video of Mahomes executing those types of steps while dropping back to pass.
“I think he just encouraged me,” Ertz said, “how aggressive he was.”
Ertz was a resource for Mahomes, too. There was a certain point, he said, when Mahomes shared that he was struggling to push off his big toe when running. Ertz had gone through that same issue, so he gave Mahomes an exercise to use and texted over a video that had worked for him.
It’s all led to this point for Mahomes and Ertz, who have exceeded expectations in their respective returns. Mahomes was cleared to be a full participant for training camp practices in late July — barely more than seven months removed from surgery.
Ertz said he texted Mahomes that day: “Bro, you’re killing it.”
“It’s not surprising why he’s so great,” Ertz said. “He attacks everything.”
A similar mentality helped lift Ertz to the verge of his own NFL comeback, too.
Ertz, whose Dec. 15 surgery was in Houston, was fully cleared by Dr. Walter Lowe to participate in football activities last month. Since then, he participated in a workout on Stanford’s campus with former Colts quarterback Andrew Luck and trains every day while weighing his NFL options.
The numbers suggest he’s ready to go again. Ertz says his GPS tracking shows his top speed is 99 percent of what it was before surgery last season, and after an offseason of strength training, his force-plate jumps show better force than before he was hurt.
“I still feel like I can make a difference in the league as a player,” said Ertz, who would be entering his 14th pro season. “And so for me, it’s just trying to figure out which situation is the best for me and my family, and determining when that is.”
Ertz said it’s now about waiting for the right opportunity. Things can change quickly with teams during training camp, so for now, he’s in a routine of spending six hours a day with route work, physical therapy and weightlifting to ensure he’s ready to step in when needed.
“I have a lot of objective data that is telling me that I’m in a great spot,” Ertz said. “So obviously I need to go out there and prove it and earn whatever role that I’m able to. And I don’t need to be promised anything — just an opportunity to compete, whenever that is. But for me, I feel this knee is not going to change the way I play the game.”
Perhaps Ertz’s best argument that he’s back to himself at this point? It could be NFL teams seeing practice highlights of Mahomes after going through a similar return-to-play process.
Ertz said he was wowed by Mahomes starting in May’s organized team activities, when the Chiefs QB did throwing drills and did some limited cutting while practicing with teammates. Recent Chiefs camp videos show that Mahomes has progressed since then.
“It’s remarkable to be able to be where he’s at at this point, with what doesn’t look like any limitations,” Ertz said. “He’s wearing the brace, obviously. I texted him. I said, ‘I wouldn’t know that you were hurt. The brace is the only thing that tells me that you had surgery.’ Other than that, it looks the same as he always does to me.”
Though Ertz has never had Mahomes as a teammate, he said he’d be watching him closely this season while knowing all he’s gone through to get back to this point.
“He’s constantly pushing the boundaries with his body, with his play, and it’s not a surprise why he’s one of the best players to ever play in the National Football League, just because of how he approaches adversity, how he approaches success,” Ertz said. “So I think that was something that I knew about him, but it was different, going through the same struggles.”

full_text:
Las Vegas QB Kirk Cousins, right, says, "I’d love for Fernando (Mendoza) to go on to an outstanding career and look back and say, ‘I think Kirk’s time together with us in the quarterback room was helpful.'" David Becker / Associated Press
HENDERSON, Nev. — Kirk Cousins is all in on the plan.
The 14-year veteran, who turns 38 on Wednesday, has a finite runway as the Las Vegas Raiders’ starting quarterback. But Cousins has been around the NFL’s results-driven business long enough to recognize tomorrows are out of reach and todays are what truly count.
So while the Raiders drafted quarterback Fernando Mendoza with the No. 1 pick with every intention of eventually giving him the keys to the franchise, it’s Cousins’ assignment to pocket them until the time is right.
“I understand what I signed up for, and we’re all in this together,” Cousins told The Athletic . “We’re just trying to help the Raiders win football games, and I don’t want to be entitled or be given something I didn’t earn. I think it’s important that the best player plays, or the one who can help the team win the most. That’s really what the perspective needs to be. If it’s not me, it’s not me. We’ll all be working together and trying to help this team win and let the chips fall where they may.
“I’d love to be a help. I’d love for Fernando to go on to an outstanding career and look back and say, ‘I think Kirk’s time together with us in the quarterback room was helpful to my development as a player.’ That’s all part of this and wanting to be an asset to this organization and this quarterback room, and that includes helping Fernando go on to have a tremendous career.”
Cousins, like the Raiders must be able to compartmentalize for this union to remain aligned. While they aren’t seriously expected to contend in a loaded AFC West, it’s vital for second-year general manager John Spytek and rookie head coach Klint Kubiak to establish their footprint and eventually their organizational identity. The Raiders entered the offseason with the most salary cap space in the league, so additions like Cousins, center Tyler Linderbaum, linebackers Quay Walker and Nakobe Dean, as well as edge rusher Kwity Paye were brought in with culture and competitiveness in mind.
And for Cousins, who has experienced life in nearly every corner of the quarterback career arc — from being thrust into a Washington QB room in 2012 with fellow rookie and No. 2 pick Robert Griffin III, to competing more heartily against Father Time at his more recent stops in Minnesota and Atlanta — Cousins has the requisite wherewithal to understand the difference between personal goals and team business.
After all, Cousins joined the Raiders in early April, knowing full well they planned to take Mendoza.
“Anytime you’re not caught off guard, that’s a good thing,” said Cousins, who was “stunned” when the Falcons selected QB Michael Penix Jr. in the 2024 draft, months after signing Cousins to a lucrative contract. “At the same time, welcome to the NFL. You’re going to have surprises. Change is always happening, and you’ve got to be able to roll with it. Those who can adapt and move forward are those who tend to last. We’ll see how it all plays out. The story is being written.”
Cousins didn’t shy away from the job despite knowing the Raiders’ priorities at the position could shift in an instant. But if Cousins gives the Raiders a chance each week, he’s far more likely to keep his perch.
Or at the very least, if the Raiders reboot with Mendoza, Cousins can prolong his career with an admirable performance in adverse conditions.
“It would seem if you’re playing good football at the quarterback position, there’s always going to be a demand for you,” Cousins said. “Just go out there and make sure you can help your football team win games, and let the chips fall where they may.”
Cousins ranks 15th all time with 298 passing touchdowns and 29th with 44,700 yards. He’s three touchdowns and 3,477 yards from jumping to 14th in each category. Cousins will also go down as a financial trailblazer, as he’s locked into his 11th consecutive season with a fully guaranteed contract.
On the other side, Cousins only has four career playoff starts, including one win, and he’s never been to back-to-back postseasons. The Raiders, who haven’t won a playoff game since January 2003, aren’t likely candidates to enhance Cousins’ postseason resume.
But they do offer familiarity. Cousins has history with Kubiak, offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko and offensive line coach Rick Dennison. Cousins said there were a couple other teams that showed interest in the offseason, though he declined to name them.
With the Pittsburgh Steelers tied to Aaron Rodgers and the Vikings choosing Kyler Murray, that conceivably left Cousins with the Raiders, New York Jets, Miami Dolphins and Arizona Cardinals as viable options with a path to start. Familiarity qualifies as an understandable difference-maker.
“It’s always interesting in this league when maybe you don’t want to change teams,” Cousins said. “But then when you do, and you meet new people and new coaches, and you learn new things, you say I can’t imagine not having met those people and having not changed teams to have those experiences. I feel much the same way here. There’s just a lot of good people and a lot of good football I’ve learned just being here. It’s been enjoyable for me.”
But the game has its merciless side, so why does Cousins still do it? He followed his best season in 2022 with a ruptured Achilles in 2023 that bled into 2024. Cousins played well down the stretch last season for the Falcons, who split with him this offseason as part of a wide-scale organizational reset. It’s truly difficult to know how much he’s got left in the tank when it’s been years since he’s had consistent, healthy playing time.
But for Cousins, the why is as pure as it gets.
“It was just the desire to compete, the desire to be part of something bigger than yourself,” Cousins said. “I’m feeling like you still have a little bit to offer. I’m enjoying the chance to be out there playing. Once you’re done, you’re done. I don’t want to live in my 40s thinking that I left some meat on the bone. I’ll probably always have that mindset to kind of maximize and keep going until it’s clear that it’s time to walk away and I have peace about that. As long as I have peace about continuing to go play, I’m going to go play.”
Cousins also has an itch to scratch with his second- and third-grade sons.
“I always say I want my boys to be able to watch me play and remember it,” Cousins said. “When they’re 15, 16, 25, to still have a good memory of it and say, ‘I remember when Dad was at practice and the games and the season.’ Good or bad, they just remember being part of it. I think that’s important.
“Having to move them, is it easy on them? No. But I also think it’s good to raise resilient kids who do hard things, and life is not just about everything going your way.”
There’s symmetry in that message as it relates to Cousins’ own journey. And whether it’s gone his way or not, he’s continued to show up. That’s the plan yet again.

full_text:
Fernando Mendoza finished 10 of 16 for 97 yards and one touchdown pass in his NFL preseason debut. Ethan Miller / Getty Images
Every preseason, like clockwork, you’ll find fans and analysts overreacting to results. But how do NFL personnel look at the preseason? I’m in total agreement with the process that former scout and current NFL Network analyst Daniel Jeremiah described in a conversation with former quarterback Chase Daniel about how to evaluate preseason production and film:
“You can absolutely help yourself and win jobs/roster spots,” Jeremiah said. “I’m saying it doesn’t provide any guarantee of regular-season success. Doesn’t mean it can’t happen. Guys like (Tony) Romo & Russell Wilson are two that come to mind. For every one of those, I could give you 10 guys that crushed preseason and didn’t do much in the regular season.”
Coaches use the preseason in combination with training camp to determine position battles and who makes the final roster. Scouts can see whether a rookie’s traits will translate in the league, but production has to be taken with context. With that in mind, let’s look at some notable rookie performances in the first round of preseason games and see what we can learn from the film.
(Since Fernando Mendoza was the No. 1 draft pick, we’ll spend more time on his film review.)
Mendoza checked several boxes debuting in the Las Vegas Raiders’ first preseason game. Kirk Cousins played the first drive, then Mendoza took over until the fourth quarter. Mendoza finished 10 of 16 for 97 yards and one touchdown pass, but the rookie looked poised, was smooth through his progressions and made aggressive throws downfield. Most importantly, he looked comfortable playing under center and showed refined footwork after playing almost his entire college career in the shotgun.
Mendoza didn’t attack the middle of the field much, but when he did, it was good. Raiders coach Klint Kubiak’s offense is predicated on exposing this area of the field. Mendoza completed all seven of his passes between the numbers for 75 yards and a touchdown.
Preseason Week 1, 9:10 remaining in the second quarter, first-and-10
On first-and-10, the Raiders came out in 21 personnel (two backs, one tight end, two receivers) and had a play-action concept called with rookie receiver Malik Benson running a deep curl.
After Mendoza’s play fake to the running back, he turned around and saw both underneath defenders drop away from each other, leaving a window for Benson.
Mendoza threw the ball with anticipation as Benson was breaking. The window would have closed up if he had thrown any later. The pass got to Benson with zip and perfect placement for a 19-yard gain. Not every quarterback is comfortable turning their back to the defense, and again, it’s not something Mendoza did at Indiana, so it was encouraging to see him turn around and quickly decipher the defensive picture.
Mendoza’s best pass might have been his last of the day, which fell incomplete.
Preseason Week 1, 15:00 remaining in the fourth quarter, third-and-7
On third-and-7, Mendoza saw the safety rotate down to cover the tight end, meaning the defense had only one safety deep.
Mendoza saw the defense was in man and made an aggressive decision to throw to Deven Thompkins running a corner route. The offense only needed seven yards, and Mendoza could have settled on shorter routes, but I like the aggressive decision to look deep.
Thompkins was open but slowed down as the ball was thrown and couldn’t come down with the catch. This play was an example of Mendoza reading the coverage, understanding where the weakness lay and taking a shot at the end zone.
Mendoza was hard on himself after the game and said he let his team down. He didn’t make any major errors, but of course, there are things that he could clean up. There were a couple of plays in which he rushed through his reads or should have pulled the trigger.
Preseason Week 1, 6:44 remaining in the second quarter, second-and-15
On this play, it appeared that Jack Bech had an option route on Mendoza’s right, while Thompkins ran a backside dig route on the opposite side.
Mendoza looked to Bech first but saw the Arizona Cardinals’ underneath defender drop toward him.
Mendoza looked to Thompkins, but he hadn’t made his break yet. Instead of letting go of the ball and throwing with anticipation, Mendoza scrambled. He picked up seven yards but also ran head-up into a defender. There is no need to take that kind of hit, especially in the preseason. He has to learn to slide.
Later in the game, the Raiders called a similar concept, and Mendoza showed instant progress.
What we learned: Mendoza is further ahead with his footwork from under center and looked comfortable going from read to read. He was aggressive in throwing the ball downfield. However, he can be a little more patient with certain reads and be ready to pull the trigger a little faster at times. There will be pressure to play him, but the Raiders need to be sure their offensive line can protect him, and they won’t know until the regular season. Mendoza is starting to show he can run the offense capably. Cousins can fend Mendoza off if he keeps the Raiders in playoff contention.
Jeremiah’s explanation of how to properly evaluate preseason was in response to Daniel saying Simpson had the most impressive outing of all rookie quarterbacks and that “it wasn’t close.” Simpson finished with an impressive stat line (21 of 25, 190 yards, two touchdown passes). He played well, but after a closer look, his performance was more in the good range than great, and there is nothing wrong with that. Simpson executed the plays called, made good decisions and was accurate.
However, much of his production came on keepers (bootlegs), and he checked the ball down a lot. He had six keepers called for him, and one of his touchdown passes was on a screen. He threw the ball short of the first-down marker in three third-down situations and only averaged 4.7 air yards per target.
The Rams only had six points going into the fourth quarter until Simpson started throwing the ball downfield. Several of his best throws of the day occurred in the fourth quarter.
Preseason Week 1, 8:05 remaining in the fourth quarter
Earlier in the game, Simpson hit a slot fade against cover 2 zone in the honey hole. On this play, the Kansas City Chiefs’ defense initially presented a one-deep safety look, which is a premium look to throw a slot fade.
However, after the snap, the defense dropped into cover 4 to the slot fade side and cover 2 to the opposite side. Simpson saw the coverage rotation and didn’t take the bait by not throwing the slot fade.
Simpson’s next read was receiver CJ Daniels running a crosser. Because of the coverage, Daniels was matched up against linebacker Kam Arnold. Arnold did a good job of rerouting Daniels, but Simpson trusted Daniels to get across his face, knowing that Arnold didn’t have safety help.
Simpson threw a perfect bullet with anticipation and placed the ball perfectly over Arnold. This was an excellent example of poise, accuracy and seeing the coverage morph.
What we learned: One of Simpson’s strengths as a prospect was his ability to execute “pro-style” concepts, including play action, and he did just that against the Chiefs. The downfield throws late in the game were impressive, though. Simpson isn’t challenging for starting reps anytime soon with Matthew Stafford healthy, but maybe he can push to be the primary backup over Stetson Bennett. Perhaps he’s earned enough trust for coach Sean McVay to take the training wheels off next game.
Allar was talked about as a potential first-round pick before last season. However, he regressed before breaking his ankle in October, which ultimately led to the Steelers picking him in the third round. Allar has first-round physical traits, but his two biggest shortcomings are decision making and accuracy. Against the Green Bay Packers, Allar finished 10 of 13 for 154 yards, two passing…

full_text:
Rookie fullback Max Bredeson might have been a fifth-round pick this spring, but he's likely to play a big role in the Vikings' run game this season. Alli Rusco / Minnesota Vikings
EAGAN, Minn. — His shaggy hair spills out over a headband. He yells. He beats his chest. He smacks his helmet with both hands as if he has entered another dimension.
Talk to the people who know Max Bredeson best, and they will confirm that he has.
These sequences, captured by the cameras, show a man consumed by a lifelong passion. His outpouring of emotion is an expression of love. These crazed scenes, which often occurred in the pregame cauldron of the “Big House” in Ann Arbor, Mich., offer a window into a path forged by beautiful irrationality.
“I don’t know where that comes from,” his father, Mike, said recently. “I think it’s just the pent-up … it’s not frustration, but it’s … desire .”
Bredeson getting @UMichFootball hyped ahead of The Game 😤 pic.twitter.com/3u12cDbhdy
— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) November 30, 2024
The Minnesota Vikings recognized the meaning behind these bursts of intensity. Their scouting evaluation, comprehensive enough to unearth the aptitude beneath that bushy head of hair, compelled the team to select Bredeson in the fifth round of the 2026 draft.
Drafting a former Michigan walk-on fullback/tight end made for a cool enough story. But the tale is even more poignant now, because as part of the team’s offensive transformation, fueled by the hiring of former Miami Dolphins offensive coordinator Frank Smith, the Vikings are handing Bredeson a hefty role.
Teammates rave about how quickly he has taken to coach Kevin O’Connell’s complex offense. Bredeson is already lining up with the first team. His responsibilities require him to line up in several spots. His assignments can even change depending on how defenders move after the snap.
“I think the most impressive part has been watching a young guy pay such attention to the details,” tight end T.J. Hockenson said. “He doesn’t just understand his job, but he understands where he fits within the scheme.”
To retain the element of surprise, the Vikings have concealed the full extent of their offensive plans. But there are still some breadcrumbs to gather.
For example, no NFL player with at least 300 snaps in 2025 motioned before the snap more than former Dolphins fullback Alec Ingold. Smith arrived in Minnesota with a charge to incorporate many of Miami’s creative tenets into the Vikings’ run game. Ingold’s status as a run-blocking fixer in that system would lead most observers to predict that Bredeson, the Vikings’ only true fullback, could occupy a similar role.
If that happens, it will signal the team’s rare level of trust in a rookie. It will also spotlight a journey worth celebrating.
“He’s what’s right about college football,” former Michigan co-offensive coordinator Steve Casula said.
It’s much more than that. Bredeson is what’s right about parenting and sibling pride and pursuing goals. His football career represents what can happen when unabashed conviction meets curiosity. Bredeson believed when others were understandably skeptical. He was willing to seek answers and commit himself to the point of exhaustion.
His family did not allow skeptics to deter him from pursuing his dream. Instead, his parents pushed. His brothers listened. All of them, successful in their chosen fields, matched his fearless chase with an incredible level of support.
“It all stems from our parents,” Bredeson’s oldest brother, Jack, said. “They gave us every opportunity, but losing was never OK.”
Bredeson’s mother, Deb, summed up their parenting approach this way: “Awards for showing up, the trophies and the juice boxes and the snack mix — yeah, we didn’t do that.”
Competitiveness courses through all of their veins. The father, Mike, played center at Illinois State, but that only scratches the surface. Deb owned a black Labrador retriever named Five Star General Patton. It became so well-trained that Deb began traveling the country for dog competitions. In 2003, Patton won the National Retriever Championship.
The boys watched their mother rise at 3 a.m. to deliver newspapers, a job to cover the dog-training expenses. They, too, found their own obsessions. Jack starred as a baseball player at Arrowhead High (Hartland, Wisc.). Their second son, Ben, became one of the best high school offensive tackles in the country.
As the youngest, Max tricycled his way to nearby basketball courts and local fields to compete with his older siblings. Football captured his heart.
Jack accepted a scholarship to Michigan, where he was a pitcher before earning a job in the New York Mets’ front office. Ben followed Jack’s trail to Michigan, but as a football player. The Baltimore Ravens drafted him in the fourth round in 2020, and he now plays left guard for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Their accomplishments fueled Max’s desire to wear the maize and blue.
“I had a tough conversation with him when he was in eighth grade,” Deb said. “I said, ‘Max, Michigan is the boys’ path. It doesn’t have to be your path. You can do anything. You can go anywhere. We will be super proud of you.’ He looked at me like I was insane.”
Max interjected: “Mom, you don’t understand. I have to be a Michigan man.”
But injuries derailed Max’s career as a high school quarterback. He responded to Michigan’s generous preferred walk-on offer with gratitude and daily effort. He peppered coaches with questions. He embraced every day of practice. He treated punt coverage duty like it would affect the future of humanity.
Max’s consistency kept him so prominently in his coaches’ minds that when former Michigan coach Jim Harbaugh approached his own father about supplementing the Wolverines’ offense with a fullback, Jack Harbaugh suggested Max as a fit.
“As parents, before that, we had planned to have a tough conversation with him,” Mike said. “He had been buried on the depth chart. And it was his second year with out-of-state tuition: $78,000. That was going to be a tough talk.”
Fortunately, the endangered position gave Max an identity. He swapped his bland No. 82 for a more menacing No. 44. He gained almost 60 pounds. These developments coincided with his growing voice in the locker room, where he was respected enough to yell, beat his chest and smack his helmet without repercussions.
Max joined Ben as a two-time Michigan captain. He carved out a niche.
“If I had to coach one more football practice for the rest of my life and pick somebody to go coach,” Casula said, “it’d be him.”
Vikings staffers might not be ready to go that far with their praise. But their respect for Bredeson is apparent in the number of snaps he gets in training camp.
Attend one of the team’s joint practices this week with the Baltimore Ravens. Keeping your eye on Bredeson is as hard as tracking a ball beneath shuffling cups. He starts there. Then he moves there. Then he returns to the starting point.
There is no hesitation, no mistake, no uncertainty. Max knows where he’s supposed to be. And he’ll get there. He always has.

full_text:
The Philadelphia Eagles traded WR A.J. Brown to the New England Patriots The Eagles traded A.J. Brown to the New England Patriots in June for a 2028 first-round pick and 2027 fifth-round pick. Jaiden Tripi / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — Walk into the Philadelphia Eagles’ stadium pro shop this week, and you’ll encounter racks of $20 sale items labeled “OBSOLETE JERSEYS.” They’re full of A.J. Brown’s No. 11 Eagles jersey — previously a popular item.
A side panel outside the stadium where an enormous banner of Brown stretched last year remains bare, ripe for fresh imaging.
In the practice facility, they’ve already made the changes.  A banner in the auditorium has been updated. Above the stage where the team holds meetings, reminders of fundamentals hang. A.J. Brown had been in an image demonstrating a specific ball security technique. That has since been replaced by an image of DeVonta Smith.
On the field, the No. 11 previously worn by Brown now belongs to young linebacker Jihaad Campbell. Right by the sales rack of Brown’s $20 jerseys, Campbell’s No. 30 jersey from his rookie season is sold at a 50 percent discount.
The Eagles have moved on to a life without Brown. The storyline dominated the five months of the offseason before the June 1 trade. Not anymore. The offense is different. The wide receiver corps has been reconfigured. His name seldom comes up in interviews.
For at least the next two days, expect to hear about Brown again. The Eagles travel to Foxborough, Mass., on Tuesday. They practice against the New England Patriots on Wednesday and Thursday ahead of Saturday’s preseason game. These are the most anticipated joint practices since the sessions became a regular part of August. Every rep between Brown and Quinyon Mitchell will be scrutinized. The offense will have a litmus test for how it looks without Brown. For at least a week, there will be reminders of the star receiver’s gravitational pull from the past four years — and a reminder for Brown of the team that offered the finest years of his career and a Super Bowl ring.
“It’s no bad blood this way — you’re talking about one of the best in the game,” Eagles edge rusher Nolan Smith said after Monday’s practice. “Y’all make it out to be this and that, but iron sharpens iron. I don’t go up against him, so I ain’t worried about it. But hopefully he don’t catch too many balls, and we do our job.”
The only time you’ll hear Brown discussed from the Eagles is when there are questions about him. The tone of the summer was set by quarterback Jalen Hurts on the first day of camp: “100 percent alignment, zero percent entitlement.” The comment was not about Brown, although the implication was clear: the Eagles must be aligned this season.
Brown does not need to be discussed to realize he’s no longer here. Watching the offense at practice each day makes it clear. For the past four seasons, the offense was built with the potential Hall of Famer in mind. It mostly worked — the Eagles won a Lombardi Trophy, made the Super Bowl twice, reached the playoffs each year, and Brown rewrote the franchise’s record books.
“I would say it was a good run,” coach Nick Sirianni said after Brown was traded. “But really excited about that (wide receivers) room that we have.”
In four seasons, Brown totaled 32.6 percent of the Eagles’ receiving yards, 27.2 percent of the targets and 25.3 percent of the receptions. That’s the void the Eagles need to fill.
DeVonta Smith is the new clear No. 1 receiver. The franchise has believed he’s been worthy of that distinction even when Brown was his teammate, and Smith’s volume is expected to rise this season. Smith was last the unquestioned top option in 2021. He said at the start of camp that he’s “a lot more mature” since then, with a better understanding of how to play. (He averaged more than 1,000 yards per season during that period.) One way to look at it is that the Eagles don’t need to replace Brown’s production; they need to replace Smith’s production if Smith is the Brown replacement.
General manager Howie Roseman traded up in the first round of last April’s NFL Draft for Makai Lemon, last season’s Biletnikoff Award winner at USC for the nation’s top college receiver. Roseman also traded for Dontayvion Wicks, who was stuck in a glut of pass catchers with Green Bay but is in line for a top-three role with the Eagles. Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore add experience, and if one emerges as part of the rotation, it provides a helpful boost. Darius Cooper has emerged as a potential option among the group of developmental options Roseman accumulated down the depth chart. The passing game also includes players from other positions, such as tight end Dallas Goedert and running back Saquon Barkley, in big roles.
It’s not going to be one-for-one swaps from the 2022-2025 offense. Roseman has spoken about building a wide receiver depth chart that resembles a basketball lineup — each member offering a different size and skill set to form a complete lineup.
“ We have a very exciting group there,” offensive coordinator Sean Mannion said. “It’s because there are so many complementary skill sets. We look for a ton of flexibility in terms of everybody (being able to) line up anywhere, and we can move people around, and it opens up a lot of exciting possibilities. That’s part of what makes this group really fun to work with. You have a lot of guys who can play off of one another in different ways.”
For most of the summer, this concept has been theoretical. Smith and Lemon missed two weeks of practices with a hamstring injury. Lemon also missed most of the spring. Smith returned to practice on a limited basis on Monday. He likely progresses toward his normal role this week in New England. Lemon has not yet returned to practice, although his running on side fields has ramped up and he appears to be progressing. When they’re back, there will be a better sense of how the receivers will look without Brown. Most of training camp has been about seeing who else could fill the void.
“Words can’t describe how valuable they are,” Hurts said of the reps for the other receivers.
Wicks and Cooper are two players who have taken the most advantage of them this summer. Wicks is expected to be a key contributor in the offense. Sirianni compared his playing style to that of six-time Pro Bowler Keenan Allen — ”I hope you know how much high praise that is,” Sirianni said — and noted the ability to separate at the top of the route, get off press coverage and the competitive zeal.
Hurts also lauded the “aggression” — in a good way — that Wicks brought to the offense. He called Wicks “twitchy,” and said Wicks “can attack the ball” and “runs great routes.” Wicks, who is 6-foot-1 and 206 pounds, averaged 36 catches for 442.7 yards and 3.7 touchdowns in three seasons with the Green Bay Packers. He never played more than 54 percent of the offensive snaps. Look for all those data points to grow this season. Barkley told ” Up & Adams” that Wicks was a “steal,” and he did not know how Roseman landed him.
“I think it’s a big opportunity for everybody in our room,” Wicks said when asked about his opportunity. “Everybody marries up with each other. Everybody can do different things. I think that helps us out individually. I think it’s going to be a fun year with this group.”
It won’t be realized until they’re together. The sooner Lemon returns, the more reasonable it is for the first-rounder to have an immediate effect on the offense. The group’s long-term outlook will depend on Lemon taking a chunk of the production-in-the-aggregate replacement strategy. Hurts has been impressed with how Lemon remains engaged during his absence and has learned from Smith.
“He might not be getting these reps, but am I in the huddle, am I feeling it, am I getting that vibe, that same energy as if I am playing and I do have my pads on?” Hurts said. “ It’s all in the preparation. (Lincoln) Riley’s always said nothing but great things about Makai…

full_text:
Rookie tight end Eli Raridon could be the Patriots' No. 2 to start the season. Eric Canha / Imagn Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Mike Vrabel stopped short of revealing whether veterans like Drake Maye would play in Saturday night’s preseason game against the Philadelphia Eagles. But the coach seemed inclined to give them a break if things go well in a pair of joint practices Wednesday and Thursday.
“Two days of joint practices with a lot of reps, I think upwards of probably 28 reps, 30 reps for the first group on each day is a good number,” Vrabel said.
In other words, it seems likely that we’ll see a lot of the team’s young players on Saturday.
With that in mind, let’s take stock of where the team’s nine drafted rookies stand with about three weeks until the regular-season opener.
As the Pats deal with a slew of injuries to their backup interior offensive linemen, Vrabel said he might try Lomu at guard. But that has yet to happen because, as Vrabel insinuated, the team does not want to stunt his development at tackle.
“I’ve got a lot of coaches that probably think differently than what you guys — and maybe me — think, and that it’s a little bigger deal, but I think Caleb’s been working hard,” Vrabel said. “He’s been trying to improve, but I think at some point we will need to (try him at guard) as well, and that’s just trying to be fair to the kid … as he’s developing and learning this game and this league.”
After injuries to Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich, the Patriots would be in a tough spot if any of their projected starters — left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker, center Jared Wilson or right guard Mike Onwenu — had to miss time. That is why they agreed to a one-year deal Monday evening with veteran Greg Van Roten, a 36-year-old who has started all 17 games at guard in each of the last three seasons for the Las Vegas Raiders (2023) and New York Giants (2024-25).
That depth should allow the Patriots to keep Lomu at tackle.
Based on Vrabel’s comments Monday, it seems Jacas still has a ways to go to make up for missing all of the team’s spring practices and the start of training camp.
“I think that it needs to be better,” Vrabel said of Jacas’ progress. “It was better on Saturday than it was in the game. We pointed some things out to him in the game, and I felt it was really cool of him to be able to make those corrections. … He was really conscious of those, and I saw those things translate in a quick, short amount of time from the meeting after the game to Saturday’s practice.”
The reality is that even if Jacas isn’t fully up to speed, the Patriots will need him, potentially even in a starting role Week 1. That’s because Harold Landry, who is supposed to be their top edge rusher, hasn’t practiced all spring or summer and remains on the physically unable to perform list.
Tight end is a difficult position for rookies, and the idea after the draft was that Raridon would have plenty of time to develop behind Julian Hill. But after Hill’s season-ending injury, Raridon has had the difficult task of trying to master all that comes with playing tight end in a complex offense. He is set for a meaningful role as the No. 2 option behind Hunter Henry.
How has Raridon handled it?
“Probably fairly well,” Vrabel said. “I think it could always be better. I think that he’s done some good things. I think he’s learning. He rarely makes the same mistake twice. If we coach him on something or he didn’t like what he did one day, he usually comes back the next day and does a decent job at it. You can see him consciously trying to do the things that we’re asking him to do, and I think we’re headed in a good direction. But (there’s) a long way to go.”
There’s a wide-open competition for the last cornerback job, and Prunty is in the mix. Carlton Davis is back at practice, but with him sidelined for a few weeks, Prunty got plenty of run with the starting defense and didn’t look dramatically out of place.
Prunty brings speed to the secondary that perhaps only Christian Gonzalez can match and has a good argument to make the roster as a developmental outside corner.
The Patriots have generated some solid depth at offensive tackle, which is great for the team but hurts Crownover’s place on the depth chart.
Lomu is the obvious choice for swing tackle behind Morgan Moses and Will Campbell, but Marcus Bryant has also had some nice moments, which has likely pushed Crownover to the fifth spot on the depth chart at tackle.
He would be well-served to develop on the practice squad, but the question could become whether the Patriots think they can get him there in late August without another team signing him to their roster.
It’s all about special teams for Obiazor. K.J. Britt played well in the preseason opener, which limited Obiazor’s playing time on defense. So, his best chance to make a case for the 53-man roster will be via special teams.
He performed fine in the preseason opener and is going to get a ton of reps in the final two preseason games.
Teams are more inclined to carry three quarterbacks now than they were five years ago, so Morton is probably on the right side of the roster bubble. But it’s far from a sure thing as a couple of big games loom.
The seventh-round pick out of Alabama was probably on the wrong side of the roster bubble before a season-ending injury to Terrell Jennings. That opened the door for Miller, who ran effectively (though not exceptionally) in the preseason opener.
He brings more speed and traditional running prowess to the No. 3 competition than Lan Larison, but Larison likely offers more upside in the passing game, presenting a tough choice for coaches.
No New England edge rusher has taken more advantage of the opportunities from Landry’s extended absence than Hutchins, who often looks the part despite being a seventh-round pick.
His explosiveness off the ball is impressive (and not a coincidence since he posted a 37-inch vertical leap), but he’ll need to add more size to stand up against the run. He probably would only be used in a specific pass-rushing role if he makes the team.
